skyline.text: Why we remember not the moment but our last remembering
What Ajay Shah learnt from a sailboat off Santa Cruz
Max Weber’s answer when he was asked to name his field

brief.head: Alone, not lonely
brief.text: Ajay Shah’s research has always needed people to argue with. But there is not enough self-reflection in the world, Amit Varma said, and solitary hobbies make room for it. {093-C06}

brief.head: The gardener’s firm
brief.text: One view runs a firm like cooking, mixing ingredients from the top. The other, Ajay Shah said, is gardening: create conditions, and let many attempts bloom or fail. {093-C07}

brief.head: Prepare, don’t plan
brief.text: Planning expects order; preparation expects chaos, Sahil Bloom tweeted. Everybody has a plan until they are punched in the mouth, Ajay Shah added, quoting Mike Tyson. {093-J23}

brief.head: Think like a crackhead
brief.text: Crackheads never say they are too broke to smoke tonight, a tweet noted. When writers ask whether they should write a book, Amit Varma says no: want it badly enough. {093-C17}

brief.head: Shrink-wrapped issues
brief.text: Find a long-debated question obvious, Gurwinder Bhogal tweeted, and you have shrunk the issue to fit your mind. Taking the tribal line, Amit Varma said, means not caring about truth. {093-C11}

thought.text: A headful of fears has no space for dreams.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, adding his own good gyan after William Faulkner’s line on courage

lead.kicker: Amit Varma opens his Good Gyan folder for Ajay Shah
lead.head: Pearls from the cesspool
body: Ajay Shah opened with a dare. Amit Varma, he said, had once claimed that Twitter is more than “the cesspool of the global mind”. “Prove it.” {093-J01}
Varma conceded much of the case. Social media went bad, he agreed, when retweets and likes began to amplify tribalism and the hunger for validation.
But a well-curated feed, he argued, gives you “the privilege to listen to the best minds in the world think aloud for your benefit every morning”. {093-C01}

His evidence was a folder. Twitter lets users sort their bookmarks, and Varma keeps one called Good Gyan for tweets that strike him as wise. He means to return to them and be enlightened. “Guess what? I never go back,” he admitted.

So he read a batch of them to Shah, who had not seen them before and answered on the spot. What he had bookmarked, Varma said, would reveal as much about him as about the tweeters. “The reader makes the tweet as much as the writer,” Shah replied.
## Seeing and believing
The first was Anais Nin’s line: “We do not see things as they are. We see things as we are.” Varma called it a profound truth, and a caution against rushing to judgment. {093-C02}
Shah came at it from the other end. He worries about post-truth thinking, in which everyone has their own truth. Planck’s formula for black body radiation, he said, is “correct to the last decimal”.
Give up the uphill search for truth, he said, and you might as well be a cat.
Varma replied that he was talking about perception, not reality. “Of course I agree with you, and of course you agree with me, right?” he said.
## Envy, courage, purpose
Montesquieu, by way of Morgan Housel, observed that being happy is easy but being happier than others is hard, because we think others happier than they are. Shah thought at once of social media.
His cure is a healthy selfishness: stay busy writing, making and building. “It’s like I am on my selfish project of make me,” he said. “Then why am I so bothered about you?” {093-C08}

William Faulkner’s line about the courage to lose sight of the shore drew a sailing story from Shah and, from Varma, a case for ignoring conventional thinking. “So you sometimes have to let go of the shore,” Varma said.
Shah offered his own: “A headful of fears has no space for dreams.”
On Nietzsche’s “why” and “how”, Shah was blunt. “Purpose is the superpower. Everything else is solvable.”
But he paired it with the Bhagavad Gita: you are obliged to try, you do not control the outcome, and the world owes you nothing.
## What to leave out

Later tweets took in doctors, AI and crackheads. The last was Pico Iyer quoting Rousseau: real wisdom is knowing which things are necessary, which are less necessary and which are “completely unnecessary to know”. {093-C13}
For that, Iyer added, you have to put your phone away. Varma pointed at Shah, who had spent half an hour before the shoot on calls about the markets and America.

Varma’s one recommendation was the essays of Paul Graham, whose tweets often land in the folder. “Just marvellous. Absolutely marvellous.” Shah, whose picks swing between none and seven, promised seven next time.

second.label: Medicine and data
second.head: Grief finds a data gap
second.deck: Amit Varma’s loss in the second COVID wave led him to a systems problem
body: Amit Varma’s father died in 2021, in the second wave of COVID. {#dad} Varma got talking with a friend who had just sold his company, and whose father had also died.

Varma decided that the real problem was data: no one had a patient’s full information in one place. Someone, he said, had to build a startup for it, and he has since heard of several people doing pieces of it. {093-S06}

The gain would be twofold. With consent, any doctor could see the whole picture. And an AI given a population’s anonymised data could spot what no single doctor can, such as a disease cropping up in Sholapur. {#sholapur}

quote.text: I just thought that the real problem here is in the data collection and having all the data.

second.caption: the missing medical data

third.head: Read, sleep, then write
body: Since the mid-1990s, Ajay Shah has written a fortnightly column for the *Business Standard*, due on Sunday afternoon. He described how it goes when it goes well. {#column}

By Saturday evening he has the idea, often after texting a few people for suggestions. Then he reads around it, pushing data and current graphs into his head, without taking notes or planning the storyline. {093-S08}
“I sort of fill my head with the question in a non-purposive way,” he said. Then he goes to sleep, and “when I wake up, I’m just so much more clear”. Between about ten and noon on Sunday, he writes.
Amit Varma, who had weekly columns for 15 years, agreed: once your brain has adapted to a deadline, “your brain will find a way”. {#fifteen}
third.caption: writing a column overnight

p2.title: The good gyan
p2.deck: Amit Varma reads tweets from his bookmarks to Ajay Shah, who hears them cold and answers on the spot

sections.label: Good Gyan 1
sections.head: Part of the equation
sections.caption: seeing things as we are
body: The first tweet carried a line from Anais Nin: “We do not see things as they are. We see things as we are.” Amit Varma called it a profound truth. {093-R05}

Think of Akira Kurosawa’s *Rashomon*, he said, in which one event is told from different points of view and each seems credible. The world is deeply complicated, and what we make of it depends on who we are.

Memory adds another twist. Preparing for his conversation with Aanchal Malhotra, who collected memories of Partition, Varma learnt that we do not pull up the same stored file each time. We recall our last remembering, then the remembering of that. “And it’s Chinese whispers all the way down.” {093-S02}
Hence his caution: take a step back, and remember that we are part of the equation. {093-C02}
## In defence of truth

Ajay Shah declared himself a conscientious objector. He worries about post-truth thinking, where everyone has their own truth and every conspiracy theory is welcome. Some knowledge is certain, he said; how social media changed the world is fuzzy ground. {093-C03}
If you prick us, he asked, do we not bleed? That holds for all seven billion people, and is no matter of opinion. {093-J18}
~ Varma’s reply was that they agreed, and were simply talking about different things: he about perception and human frailty, Shah about the nature of the world.

quote.text: the most interesting puzzle inside our minds is learning how to attach uncertainty around each of the things that we think are true

sections.label: Good Gyan 2 and 3
sections.head: Five years, five metres
sections.caption: reading old work, and reading wide
body: Peyman Milanfar tweeted that a tech researcher reading nothing more than five years old can be sure their work will be forgotten in five years. Ajay Shah agreed: in computer science, “we reinvent the same thing again and again and we do it badly”.
He likes Emacs because, at fifty years old, it has clarity of design and bulletproof code; much modern code is disposable.
Amit Varma added that old work matters even when obsolete: there has been little progress in philosophy since Plato, and a physicist should still go back to Newton. {#plato}
Constraints taught lessons too. The people who put an Apollo lunar lander on the moon had 64 kilobytes of RAM, Shah said. {#apollo}
## Beyond the silo

Shahab Bakhtiari extended the rule from time to space: read nothing five metres away from you, metaphorically, and your work will be forgotten five metres away. Breadth, Shah said, makes you deeper. {093-C05}

He had recently read a paper on industrial policy for developing countries by a narrow economist ignorant of state capability and public choice theory, when the essence of development is that the state is broken. {093-S09}
~ Max Weber, in another tweet from Milanfar, was once asked his field. “I am not a donkey, I don’t have a field.” {#weber}

quote.text: If you narrowly write papers on superconductivity, they’ll only be read by the superconductivity gang.

sections.label: Good Gyan 6
sections.head: Happier than thou
sections.caption: envy and the project of me
body: Morgan Housel tweeted a line from Montesquieu: wishing to be happy is easily accomplished, but wishing to be happier than other people is always difficult, “for we believe others to be happier than they are”. {093-R15}
Ajay Shah thought at once of social media and its curated Eiffel Tower pictures. Our real selves, Amit Varma said, now compete with the projected selves of others.
Shah’s cure is selfishness of a healthy kind. He has things to write, make and build, so why worry about anyone else’s success? Envy, he said, is mostly a waste of time. {093-C08}
## The whole package
Varma recalled Naval Ravikant’s test: before envying someone, imagine accepting the whole package of them. Applying it, Varma said, he could find no one he would trade places with.

Downtime matters for learning too. Working memory holds only about four chunks, Varma said, so forcing it brings frustration. “The learning happens where you’re chilling, you’re not even thinking about it consciously. Maybe you’re sleeping.” {093-C09}
~ His tip, learnt from people who use the calendar well, Shah among them: schedule free time as well as the busy bits.

quote.text: Resentment is like taking poison and hoping the other person dies.

sections.label: Good Gyan 9
sections.head: Complain less, cheer early
sections.caption: whiners and new ideas
body: Gurwinder Bhogal, a thinker Amit Varma first noticed for his Twitter megathreads, tweeted that an easy way to become less unlikable is to stop complaining. Fix the problem, ask for help, or accept that complaining only pollutes the atmosphere with bitterness. {093-R21}
Varma has made cutting out negativity almost a mission of his life. Get such people out of your life, he said, “as brutally as you can”.
Ajay Shah added the positive half. When people around him come up with an idea, he goes out of his way to support it; his fifteen criticisms can come later. {093-C10}
“We are made out of the responses that other people give our ideas,” he said.
## Serenity and feedback
He offered a prayer he traced to “maybe some Christian sources”: strength to change what he can, serenity to accept what he can’t, and the wisdom to know the difference. {093-J22}
Varma’s rider was about delivery. As a generalisation, he said, men often take harsh criticism as a personal affront, while women turn it on themselves, so rife is impostor syndrome.
~ Whenever he gives feedback, he said, he tries to keep that in mind.

quote.text: emotional encouragement is just so disproportionately important at the point of inception.

sections.label: Good Gyan 11
sections.head: Fire first, fruit later
sections.caption: purpose and the Gita
body: Visakan Veerasamy, whom Amit Varma has often been urged to invite onto his podcast, tweeted Nietzsche: “he who has a why to live for can bear with almost any how”. {#nietzsche}
Ajay Shah did not hesitate. “Purpose is the superpower. Everything else is solvable.” People fixate on projects and resources, he said, but the fire is the key. {093-C12}

Varma pushed back. Purpose can be a burden. A long game, which both of them are playing, may bring no gratification at all, while someone with no higher purpose, rising to vice president of a bank and taking fancy vacations, can be happy.
## Try, then let go
Shah’s answer was to marry purpose to the Bhagavad Gita: you are obliged to try, but you cannot control what is external. {#gita}

Varma pressed: does it bring happiness? Only if you stop asking for the fruit of the labour, Shah said. Measure a purpose by its outcome and you invite pain, “because the world owes you nothing”. The bigger the purpose, the higher the chance it will crash and burn.
~ Varma had put the alternative bluntly: no purpose at all, and “you just go with the groove”.

quote.text: if you define it in a goal orientation, then you’re setting yourself up for potentially a lot of pain

sections.label: Good Gyan 14 and 15
sections.head: Second opinion: the AI
sections.caption: doctors, patients and machines
body: A doctor’s sign told patients not to confuse their Google search with a medical degree. Tiffany Ryder, in a tweet Amit Varma agreed with, said any doctor threatened by patients using WebMD should have studied harder. {#webmd}

Lancelot Pinto, the pulmonologist, went further: no one understands what patients are going through better than they do, so doctors should encourage them to read up rather than gaslight them. {093-R29}
Ajay Shah added an Indian problem: most doctors do not read the literature. Patients read Google or Google Scholar; the doctors almost never read Google Scholar.
## The docket and the machine
His hope is AI. Research, he said, finds that an AI fed a complete patient history in a formal way beats almost all the doctors of the world. {093-C15}

So nurses and doctors could spend hours compiling each patient’s full history into a docket for the AI. It may be the only way, Shah said, to solve both the quantity and the quality of India’s doctors.
Varma, a super-optimist about AI, gave his usual caveat. “Don’t let it become a crutch. Let it be a tool.” {093-C14}
~ Shah, for his part, is not worried that AI will suppress the imagination: creative sparks, he believes, lie deep inside the human mind.

quote.text: when the complete patient history is given to the AI in a formal way, it beats almost all the doctors of the world.

side.boxText: Twitter lets you sort bookmarks into folders. Amit Varma keeps one called Good Gyan, for tweets that strike him as wise. He saves them to be enlightened later, and never goes back. This episode finally put the folder to use. {093-S01}

contQuote.text: Real wisdom is not the knowledge of everything, but the knowledge of which things in life are necessary, which are less necessary, and which are completely unnecessary to know.

p3.title: Told between tweets
p3.deck: A maestro, a sailboat, a group chat and a ten-hour podcast

stories.start: So Barigula Malikansa was called by this Raja to perform at this particular venue
stories.end: At which point Barigulamalikan Sab said to him, Ja Sakhana Waisagana
stories.caption: Bade Ghulam Ali Khan’s vegetarian weekend
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a maestro, a Raja and a vegetarian weekend
stories.head: Three days of cabbage, one concert
body: A Raja once invited Bade Ghulam Ali Khan to perform at his venue. The concert was on a Sunday, but the singer arrived on Friday and was given the best hospitality.
Except that the food was vegetarian. Perhaps, the maestro thought, it was some Friday thing, and he ate what came: cabbage, aloo gobi and the like.
On Saturday, the same. On Sunday, the same. Amit Varma, telling the story, noted for the record that he and Ajay Shah are both ardent carnivores.

Khan gave his performance. Afterwards the Raja came to him. He had heard the maestro sing here, and there, and there again, he said, and those performances were mystical, magical: he had felt the oceans would part if Khan sang before them.
Then came the verdict. “Today it was good, but it didn’t quite have that flavour.” {093-S04}
Khan answered with a rhyming one-liner that tied his singing to the food he had been given: *Jaisa khana, waisa gaana*. As the food, so the song.

Varma told it straight after Shah had recalled the film *Ninotchka*, in which a humourless Russian communist in a Paris restaurant orders boiled cabbage and beet, and the waiter replies: “Ma’am, this is a restaurant, not a meadow.” {093-J06}
~ The anecdote landed between two tweets: Max Weber’s refusal to be a donkey with a field, and Gurwinder Bhogal’s advice to stop complaining. The maestro had saved his complaint for the punchline.
stories.why: What goes in shapes what comes out. A host may lavish everything on a guest, but starve an artist of what feeds him and he cannot be expected to make magic. This time, the oceans stayed where they were.

stories.start: Uh a friend of mine is a faculty member at UC Santa Cruz
stories.end: you you can just keep going forever on the back of uh the wind
stories.caption: the wind off Santa Cruz
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah answers Faulkner from a sailboat
stories.head: Gone with the wind
body: William Faulkner, quoted in a tweet, said you cannot swim for new horizons unless you have the courage to lose sight of the shore. {#faulkner} Asked what he made of it, Ajay Shah told a story.
A friend who teaches at UC Santa Cruz once took Shah and Ila out on a sailboat. The wind began pushing them away from Santa Cruz, and after a while the enormity of it hit him.
“You mean if we do absolutely nothing, the wind will just take this boat all the way out to Hawaii?” he asked. “Yeah, pretty much,” said his friend. {093-S03}
~ It was an eerie feeling, Shah said: the boat could just keep going forever. Amit Varma teased him for taking a metaphor literally, having read an earlier, literal tweet as a metaphor.
stories.why: Open water has no natural stopping point. That is what makes leaving the shore unsettling, and why, in Faulkner’s line, it takes courage. Shah, for his part, says he never stayed stuck in one field.

stories.start: I used to be part of a WhatsApp of people both you
stories.end: they're whining, whining, whining all the time and it's a race to the bottom
stories.caption: the WhatsApp group of whiners
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the group chat he walked out of
stories.head: Leave, and you’re the topic
body: Amit Varma was once part of a WhatsApp group of people both he and Ajay Shah know. All they did all day, he said, was bitch about other people.
By his count, ninety per cent of their talk was bitching about others, mutual friends included. So Varma left the group. {093-S05}
He later came to know that, once he was gone, they bitched about him. He was not surprised.
It is the same habit, he said, as Twitter’s screenshot-and-dunk, and it is deeply toxic. When complainers come together, they whine all the time, and it becomes a race to the bottom. {#bottom}
~ Time is limited, Varma said. “Do something useful with that time.”
stories.why: Groups of complainers sink together, and whoever leaves becomes the next target. Varma’s answer is to keep company with people who, when you share a new idea, help you think it through instead of reaching for a “but”.

stories.start: Like the scene in the unseen where we have done a ten hour episode
stories.end: short attention spans, do twenty minute episodes, which is how I started
stories.caption: the ten-hour episode
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the podcast rule he chose to ignore
stories.head: Twenty minutes became ten hours
body: When Amit Varma began his podcast *The Seen and the Unseen*, its episodes ran twenty minutes. That was the conventional thinking: attention spans are short. {093-S07}
He has since recorded long oral-history episodes of eight, nine and even ten hours, which he would never have done had he let convention hold him down.

He told this after a tweet by the poet Maya C Popa quoting William Faulkner on the courage to lose sight of the shore. To do anything good, Varma said, you must get conventional thinking out of the way.
“Too often we are restrained by the way that something is done,” he said. Sometimes you have to let go of the shore, and have faith in yourself. {093-C18}
~ Varma calls Popa a fine poetry editor whose Twitter feed is “awesome”.
stories.why: Many of the rules we follow are inherited rather than tested. Good work often needs you to set them aside and trust yourself, which is what losing sight of the shore meant for Varma.
stories.postscript: Varma then asked Ajay Shah which oceans he had fallen in love with. “Metaphorical question,” he warned, “so don’t tell me Pacific.”

quiz.q: Whose line did Amit Varma read first: “We do not see things as they are”?
quiz.a: Anais Nin’s, which Varma paired with Akira Kurosawa’s film *Rashomon*.

quiz.q: If we give up the uphill search for truth, what might we as well be?
quiz.a: A cat, since cats never try to work out black body radiation.

quiz.q: How much RAM did the Apollo lunar lander have, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: 64 kilobytes, a constraint that pushed its makers to deep insight.

quiz.q: What did the Raja tell Bade Ghulam Ali Khan after a weekend of vegetarian food?
quiz.a: That his singing was good, but didn’t quite have that flavour.

quiz.q: What does Ajay Shah do on Saturday night before writing his Sunday column?
quiz.a: He fills his head with the question, without notes, then sleeps on it.

quiz.q: Before envying someone, what did Naval Ravikant suggest imagining, as Amit Varma recalled?
quiz.a: Accepting their whole package, not just the thing you envy them for.
